title: Horton Castle · Writing a case study

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: So we’ll need to think about our interview questions and fix times and places for the meetings. It’s all going to take a lot of time.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Mmm. And if we can, we should ask our interviewees if they can bring along some numerical data that we can add to support our findings.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: I think we have plenty of those already. But Dr Baker also said we have to establish with our interviewees whether we can identify them in our case study, or whether they want to be anonymous.

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: Oh, I wouldn’t have thought of that.

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: OK, once we’ve got all this information, I suppose we have to analyse it.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Yes, put it all together and choose what’s relevant to the problem we’re focusing on, and analyse that carefully to find out if we can identify any trends or regularities there. That’s the main thing at this stage, rather than concentrating on details or lots of facts.

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: OK. And then once we’ve analysed that, what next?

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Well, then we need to think about what we do with the data we’ve selected to make it as clear as possible to our readers. Things like graphs, or tables, or charts.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Then the case study itself is mostly quite standard; we begin by presenting the problem, and giving some background, then go through the main sections, but the thing that surprised me is that in a normal report we’d end with some suggestions to deal with the problem or need we identified, but in a case study we end up with a question or a series of questions to our readers, and they decide what ought to be done.
